entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen33744" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33745" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33746" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33746" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33745" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33747" type="x-p"/> This chapter begins with threatening some hostile invasion in short and broken sentences, full of rapidity, and expressive of sudden danger and alarm: "The trumpet to thy mouth; he cometh as an eagle," <reference osisRef="Hos.8.1">Hos 8:1</reference>. And why? For their hypocrisy, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.2">Hos 8:2</reference>; iniquity, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.3">Hos 8:3</reference>; treason (see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.13">2Kgs 15:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.17">2Kgs 15:17</reference>) and idolatry, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.4">Hos 8:4</reference>; particularly the worshipping of the calves of Dan and Bethel, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.5">Hos 8:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.6">Hos 8:6</reference>. The folly and unprofitableness of pursuing evil courses is then set forth in brief but very emphatic terms. The labor of the wicked is vain, like sowing of the wind; and the fruit of it destructive as the whirlwind. Like corn blighted in the bud, their toil shall have no recompense; or if it should have a little, their enemies shell devour it, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.7">Hos 8:7</reference>. They themselves, too, shall suffer the same fate, and shall be treated by the nations of Assyria and Egypt as the vile sherds of a broken vessel, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.8">Hos 8:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.9">Hos 8:9</reference>. Their incorrigible idolatry is again declared to be the cause of their approaching captivity under the king of Assyria. And as they delighted in idolatrous altars, there they shall have these in abundance, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.10-Hos.8.14">Hos 8:10-14</reference>. The last words contain a prediction of the destruction of the fenced cities of Judah, because the people trusted in these for deliverance, and not in the Lord their God. <div eID="gen33747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33748" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen33748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33749" type="x-p"/> Set the trumpet to thy mouth - Sound another alarm. Let them know that an enemy is fast approaching. <div eID="gen33749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33750" type="x-p"/> As an eagle against the house of the Lord - of this be a prophecy against Judah, as some have supposed, then by the eagle Nebuchadnezzar is meant, who is often compared to this king of birds. See <reference osisRef="Eze.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.40">Jer 48:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.22">Jer 49:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.4">Dan 7:4</reference>. <div eID="gen33750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33751" type="x-p"/> But if the prophecy be against Israel, which is the most likely, then Shalmaneser, king of Assyria, is intended, who, for his rapidity, avarice, rapacity, and strength, is fitly compared to this royal bird. He is represented here as hovering over the house of God, as the eagle does over the prey which he has just espied, and on which he is immediately to pounce.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen33756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33757" type="x-p"/> Thy calf, O Samaria, hath cast thee off - Bishop Newcome translates: "Remove far from thee thy calf, O Samaria!" Abandon thy idolatry; for my anger is kindled against thee. <div eID="gen33757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33758" type="x-p"/> How long will it be ere they attain to innocency? - How long will ye continue your guilty practices? When shall it be said that ye are from these vices? The calf or ox, which was the object of the idolatrous worship of the Israelites, was a supreme deity in Egypt; and it was there they learned this idolatry. A white ox was worshipped under the name of Apis, at Memphis; and another ox under the name of Mnevis, was worshipped at On, or Heliopolis. To Osiris the males of this genus were consecrated, and the females to Isis. It is a most ancient superstition, and still prevails in the East. The cow is a most sacred animal among the Hindoos.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen33758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33759" type="x-p"/> The workman made it; therefore it is not God - As God signifies the supreme eternal Good, the Creator and Upholder of all things, therefore the workman cannot make Him who made all things. This is an overwhelming argument against all idols. Nothing need be added. The workman has made them; therefore they are not God.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen33759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33760" type="x-p"/> They have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind - As the husbandman reaps the same kind of grain which he has sown, but in far greater abundance, thirty, sixty, or one hundred fold; so he who sows the wind shall have a whirlwind to reap. The vental seed shall be multiplied into a tempest so they who sow the seed of unrighteousness shall reap a harvest of judgment. This is a fine, bold, and energetic metaphor. <div eID="gen33760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33761" type="x-p"/> It hath no stalk - Nothing that can yield a blossom. If it have a blossom that blossom shall not yield fruit; if there be fruit, the sower shall not enjoy it, for strangers shall eat it. The meaning is, the labors of this people shall be utterly unprofitable and vain.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen33761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33762" type="x-p"/> Now shall they be among the Gentiles - They shall be carried into captivity, and there be as a vessel wherein there is no pleasure; one soiled, unclean, infectious, to be despised, abhorred, not used. The allusion is to a rotten, corrupted skin-bottle; a bottle made of goat, deer, or calf hide, still commonly used in Asia and Africa. Some of them are splendidly ornamented. This is the case with one now before me made of a goat's skin well dressed, variously painted, and ornamented with leather fringes, tassels, etc. In such a bottle there might be pleasure; but the Israelites are compared to such a bottle, rough, ill-dressed, not ornamented, old, musty, and putrid. This shows the force of the comparison.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen33762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33763" type="x-p"/> They are gone up to Assyria - For succor. <div eID="gen33763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33764" type="x-p"/> A wild ass alone by himself - Like that animal, jealous of its liberty, and suffering no rival. If we may credit Pliny and others, one male wild ass will keep a whole flock of females to himself, suffer no other to approach them, and even bite off the genitals of the colts, lest in process of time they should become his rivals. "Mares singuli faeminarum gregibus imperitant; timent libidinis aemulos, et ideo gravidas custodiunt, morsuque natos mares castrant." - Hist. Nat., lib. viii., c. 30. The Israelites, with all this selfishness and love of liberty, took no step that did not necessarily lead to their thraldom and destruction. <div eID="gen33764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33765" type="x-p"/> Ephraim hath hired lovers - Hath subsidized the neighboring heathen states.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen33766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33767" type="x-p"/> Many altars to sin - Though it does not appear that the Jews in Babylon were obliged to worship the idols of the country, except in the case mentioned by Daniel, yet it was far otherwise with the Israelites in Assyria, and the other countries of their dispersion. Because they had made many altars to sin while they were in their own land, they were obliged to continue in the land of their captivity a similar system of idolatry against their will. Thus they felt and saw the evil of their idolatry, without power to help themselves.

navigation_sections.content_osis: <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33745" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33746" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33746" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33745" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33747" type="x-p"/> This chapter begins with threatening some hostile invasion in short and broken sentences, full of rapidity, and expressive of sudden danger and alarm: "The trumpet to thy mouth; he cometh as an eagle," <reference osisRef="Hos.8.1">Hos 8:1</reference>. And why? For their hypocrisy, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.2">Hos 8:2</reference>; iniquity, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.3">Hos 8:3</reference>; treason (see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.13">2Kgs 15:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.17">2Kgs 15:17</reference>) and idolatry, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.4">Hos 8:4</reference>; particularly the worshipping of the calves of Dan and Bethel, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.5">Hos 8:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.6">Hos 8:6</reference>. The folly and unprofitableness of pursuing evil courses is then set forth in brief but very emphatic terms. The labor of the wicked is vain, like sowing of the wind; and the fruit of it destructive as the whirlwind. Like corn blighted in the bud, their toil shall have no recompense; or if it should have a little, their enemies shell devour it, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.7">Hos 8:7</reference>. They themselves, too, shall suffer the same fate, and shall be treated by the nations of Assyria and Egypt as the vile sherds of a broken vessel, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.8">Hos 8:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.9">Hos 8:9</reference>. Their incorrigible idolatry is again declared to be the cause of their approaching captivity under the king of Assyria. And as they delighted in idolatrous altars, there they shall have these in abundance, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.10-Hos.8.14">Hos 8:10-14</reference>. The last words contain a prediction of the destruction of the fenced cities of Judah, because the people trusted in these for deliverance, and not in the Lord their God. <div eID="gen33747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33748" type="x-p"/>
